analysis.one_liner: Requires meat and poultry to be traceable from farm to store so contaminated food can be quickly tracked to its source.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote: introduced with no cosponsors, it sat in the Senate Agriculture Committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have amended federal meat and poultry inspection laws to require that every animal and every cut of meat or poultry shipped across state lines be identified in a way that lets the Agriculture Department trace it backward to every farm or feedlot it passed through and forward to the consumer. It would let the USDA bar untraceable animals from slaughterhouses, require businesses to keep accurate purchase and sale records open to inspection, and make it illegal to falsify or destroy those records. The goal is faster, more precise recalls when contaminated meat or poultry reaches the market.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers of meat and poultry. When outbreaks of E. coli, salmonella, or other contamination occur, a traceability system lets investigators pinpoint the source farm, plant, or lot quickly, narrowing recalls and shortening the time contaminated product sits on shelves. It also gives honest producers a way to be cleared quickly when they are not the source.

how_it_helps.text: Requires that animals be identified so USDA can trace each animal or group back to every location where it was held before slaughter, and trace carcasses and meat products forward through processing and distribution to the ultimate consumer.
Lets the Secretary of Agriculture prohibit or restrict entry of unidentifiable animals into slaughtering establishments, so meat entering the food supply cannot bypass the system.

Requires businesses to keep accurate purchase, sale, and identification records open to USDA inspection, and makes falsifying information or altering or destroying identification records illegal — closing routes by which tainted product could not be traced.
Creates a traceability system covering all stages of production, processing, and distribution of meat and poultry products, so a recall can be targeted instead of broad.

analysis.who_pays: Meatpackers, poultry processors, and livestock and poultry producers, who would bear the cost of identification devices, recordkeeping, and audits across every animal and product moving in interstate commerce. Some of that cost would likely be passed through to meat prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes significant recordkeeping and identification costs on slaughterhouses, processors, and farms of all sizes, and it leaves the details — including what identification devices are acceptable — entirely to the discretion of the Secretary of Agriculture, with no explicit accommodations for small farms.
Traceability only pays off when a contamination event occurs; it does not itself prevent pathogens from entering the food supply, so costs are borne every day while the benefit is episodic.
Compliance costs concentrated on thousands of independent producers could fall hardest on smaller operations and would likely show up in meat prices for consumers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is real but conditional: better traceability means faster, narrower recalls during outbreaks like the recurring E. coli events in ground beef, protecting consumers and sparing unaffected producers. The cost is certain and spread across the meat and poultry supply chain. The design is thin — it delegates nearly everything to USDA rulemaking and offers no cost relief for small producers — so even a supporter would acknowledge the burden was underspecified.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Schumer introduced the bill on May 3, 2007; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.
No further action was taken — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, with the bill still in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Meatpackers, poultry processors, and livestock producers avoided new identification and recordkeeping requirements; consumers never got the traceability protections the bill promised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Meat and poultry processors and producers

for.name: Sen. Charles Schumer
for.role: U.S. Senator from New York; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Agriculture Committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no position positions were recorded; it had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: Slaughterhouses and processors would have to identify every animal and carcass, keep auditable purchase and sale records, and open their records to USDA inspection — compliance costs that fall on the industry. The industry avoided these costs when the bill died, while consumers went without faster, narrower recalls.

Farmers would need to identify animals so their movement before slaughter could be traced, with costs likely hardest on smaller operations. The bill offered no cost-sharing or small-producer exemptions.
A mandatory animal identification and recordkeeping system would have created demand for ear tags, electronic identification devices, and record systems. That benefit never materialized.
